extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of American journalism history; general readers interested in Revolutionary-era newspapers
extracted.subtask_description: Standards, constraints, and performance characteristics of American newspapers during the Revolutionary period (production, format, editorial stance, distribution, and news-gathering). Useful for evaluating or reproducing period newspapers or understanding their historical functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political persuasion / partisanship
rubrics_metrics.description: Newspapers were described by their allegiance (Patriot/Whig vs Tory/Royalist) and often served as organs of propaganda for one side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Pennsylvania Journal, Gazette, and Packet were Patriot; papers like the Pennsylvania Evening Post and Royal Pennsylvania Gazette were Tory. Partisanship shaped content, survival, and consequences (seizure of presses, exile, loss of property). Papers sometimes 'turned coat' (e.g., Towne's Evening Post) or were suppressed when opposing forces occupied towns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency of publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers varied in frequency: mostly weeklies, with some semiweeklies, triweeklies, and the earliest attempts at dailies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publication schedules could change (semiweekly/triweekly shifts); towns arranged friendly distribution of publication days among papers (e.g., New York papers staggered Monday–Saturday). Frequency affected timeliness and role (e.g., semiweeklies at the war's end in New York and Philadelphia).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and news-gathering methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage relied largely on chance private letters, official messages, and clippings from other newspapers; there was no organized reporting system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: slow, haphazard reporting and regional lags in battle reports (Lexington/Concord printed weeks later in some towns). Exceptions included the syndicated 'Journal of Occurrences' and occasional 'extras' or advancing publication days to get important news out sooner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syndication and content-sharing
rubrics_metrics.description: Extent to which papers copied material and ran syndicated columns or widely reprinted essays and reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Journal of Occurrences' was a notable early syndicated column distributed across colonies. Political essays (e.g., Dickinson's 'Letters', Paine's writings) were reprinted 'nearly immediately' in many papers, increasing reach and influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of newspapers for propaganda and political persuasion
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers and pamphlets were vehicles for shaping public opinion and mobilizing support or discouragement (propaganda).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Paine's Common Sense and the Crisis hugely swayed public opinion; many papers devoted a large share of non-ad space to war and committee activities, serving semi-official propaganda roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification and reliability / susceptibility to rumor
rubrics_metrics.description: Given irregular communications, newspapers were prone to false or premature reports and rumors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustration: a month-old report reaching New York claimed France and Spain were at war with Britain. Reliance on delayed English newspapers and circuitous post routes increased misinformation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordination with authorities and official promulgation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publications cooperated with military or civil authorities to publish orders and propaganda.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a 'combination-daily' (e.g., New York papers in 1779) was set up possibly with military cooperation for promulgation of orders; such cooperation influenced content and continuity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Continuity and resilience under occupation or military threat
rubrics_metrics.description: Ability of a paper to continue, suspend, relocate, or resume publication during military occupations, evacuations, or capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Rivington ceased publication after the war but ran a bookstore; some printers buried their press (Solomon Southwick) and later exhumed it; presses, types, and plants were sometimes seized and printed aboard ships (John H. Holt's Virginia Gazette). Many papers suspended during occupations and were resumed after the British left.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and page size constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Physical page size and format were influenced by paper scarcity; some large demy sheets reverted to foolscap or smaller formats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scarcity of paper during the war checked tendencies toward larger pages; files often show frequent changes in size and paper quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Type choices and typographic display
rubrics_metrics.description: Trends in type size and face (use of smaller type e.g., minion, occasional blacker faces) and limited use of typographic emphasis for news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Generally little thought of news display, but Rivington sometimes set the most important news in a larger type (leaded pica). Minion became common; a few papers used blacker/extended faces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of illustrations and symbolic cuts
rubrics_metrics.description: Limited use of illustrations, usually symbolic nameplate cuts, stock advertising cuts, and occasional blocks for dramatic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Join or Die' snake used in Massachusetts Spy heading; Connecticut Courant used a comet diagram; Boston Gazette used coffin-shaped blocks and death's-heads to illustrate the 'massacre' story (blocks cut by Paul Revere). Overall, illustration was rare and symbolic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper quality and supply management
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality, color, and permanence of paper were affected by wartime shortage and import restrictions; domestic milling and rag collection became essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Paper was often rough, blotched, gray, or blued to improve appearance. Non-importation and war cut off imported paper; states offered subsidies, printers built mills (Connecticut Courant, Goddard), and public appeals urged saving rags as a patriotic duty (Massachusetts House resolution). Prices for rags rose dramatically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local production and technological innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Domestic manufacture of presses, type, and paper increased in response to import restrictions and patriotic spurring.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Isaac Doolittle built a mahogany press for Goddard in 1769; typefounders (Abel Buell, Christopher Sower, Justus Fox, Jacob Bay) and local papermills sprang up to meet demand increased by non-importation agreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special issues / extras for major events
rubrics_metrics.description: Issuing broadsides or extras and advancing publication days to disseminate major news promptly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Boston papers united for a broadside extra upon repeal of the Stamp Act (May 16, 1766); Pennsylvania Packet and others issued extras during the war; occasional advancement of publication day to beat competitors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial content mix (news, essays, official notices, advertising)
rubrics_metrics.description: Papers combined political essays, committee/town meeting resolutions, military news, official proclamations, and advertising; war topics dominated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Ninety percent of non-ad space in some war issues (New York Journal) was devoted to war matters. Papers also published essays by notable writers (Dickinson, Paine) and printed proclamations and committee doings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic viability and advertising dependence
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertising revenue and commercial activities (bookstores, printing contracts) were important for a paper's survival and character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Pennsylvania Packet was 'crowded with advertising' and Dunlap ran a book/publishing business; printers sometimes also ran coffee-houses, insurance businesses, or were official printers to the Continental Congress.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roles and identities of editors/publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors and publishers often held multiple civic, military, or commercial roles that shaped their papers and decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: William Bradford III served as a military officer and postmaster, Paine was a contributing editor and pamphleteer, Mary K. Goddard ran her brother's Maryland Journal and was postmistress. Such roles influenced editorial choices and resilience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distribution logistics and postal reliability
rubrics_metrics.description: Reliability of the postal system and physical distribution routes heavily affected news flow and timeliness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parliamentary post ended in 1775; the 'constitutional post' was inadequate. Military operations increased obstacles; postriders used roundabout routes and occasional private letter carriers were advertised to carry dispatches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence and legal/political protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Degree to which printers could assert freedom of the press, appeal to governmental protection, or were subjected to mob violence or official rebuke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: William Goddard successfully demanded state protection when threatened by the Whig Club; he later was mobbed for publishing an article and forced to publish a recantation. Instances show tensions between popular political pressure and legal protections.
